The basal metabolic rate of Great spotted woodpecker (Dendrocopos major) provides a useful window into its energetic physiology. Respirometry trials conducted on resting, post-absorptive adults under controlled thermal conditions have documented a maximum oxygen consumption of 161 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 161 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the ambient temperature is maintained at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This relatively high metabolic rate, measured during the thermoneutral zone, reflects the considerable energetic demands associated with the species' active foraging lifestyle and its routine cavity-excavating behaviour, which requires substantial pectoral muscle power. Comparative data from other picid species of similar body mass suggest that this value falls within the expected range for a medium-sized woodpecker, though it is somewhat elevated compared to more sedentary congeners. The measurement underscores the tight linkage between metabolic capacity and the demanding structural modifications of the cranial and cervical musculature typical of the family. Field-based estimates of resting metabolism in free-living individuals, though more variable, corroborate this laboratory finding and emphasize the species' reliance on a high-energy diet of wood-boring beetle larvae and ant pupae to sustain such rates.

Reproductive output in Great spotted woodpecker is naturally expressed through the combination of clutch size and the frequency of nesting attempts. Females typically lay a single clutch of 5 or 6 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 5 or 6 eggs per nesting attempt] and, under favorable conditions in temperate deciduous forests, will attempt approximately 1.1 broods per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.1 broods per year]. This relatively modest annual reproductive rate, observed when individuals are maintaining a body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], is characteristic of a species that invests heavily in the prolonged care of altricial young within a defended territory. The incubation period itself demands constant attention from both parents, and the hatchlings emerge in a highly altricial state, requiring around three weeks of intensive brooding and provisioning before they are capable of fledging. The thermal regime of the nesting cavity, typically maintained near 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C] during the brooding phase, is critical for embryonic development and for the early growth of the nestlings, underscoring the importance of cavity insulation in this species' life-history strategy.

The physical dimensions of Great spotted woodpecker at key life stages differ markedly between the sexes, a pattern reflecting its moderate sexual size dimorphism. Newly hatched nestlings, emerging from eggs incubated at 39 °C [T = 39 °C], are remarkably small, weighing approximately 5.7 grams [Wwb = approximately 5.7 grams] upon hatching. This initial mass is typical for a picid of this size and places the hatchling in a highly dependent state, requiring rigorous parental provisioning. As development proceeds over the subsequent weeks, the divergence between males and females becomes increasingly apparent. The ultimate wet weight attained by adult females in the wild is approximately 70.85 grams [Wwi = approximately 70.85 grams], a figure derived from large-scale ringing datasets and museum specimen series. In contrast, adult males are consistently heavier, with a recorded maximum wet weight of 80 grams [Wwi = 80 grams], a difference that is likely related to the demands of male-male competition for breeding territories and the physical exertion involved in drumming displays and cavity excavation. This dimorphism is further reflected in wing length and bill dimensions, though the body mass difference remains the most robust metric for field sexing.

Developmental timing in Great spotted woodpecker is tightly linked to thermal conditions within the nest cavity. The incubation period, during which eggs are maintained at a mean temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], results in the emergence of the altricial hatchlings after 13.5 days [ab = 13.5 days]. This duration is consistent with the incubation periods reported for other medium-sized woodpeckers in the Palearctic and reflects the balance between the rate of embryonic development and the thermal properties of the nesting substrate. Following hatching, the nestling phase is a period of extremely rapid mass gain and feather development. The time since birth at fledging, when the young first achieve sustained flight and leave the cavity, is typically 21 days [tx = typically 21 days] at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This relatively brief nestling period, measured under the stable thermal conditions of an active nest (41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]), is characteristic of a species that faces significant predation risk from arboreal mammals and larger avian predators, favoring a strategy of rapid development and early departure from the vulnerable nest site.

The pace of life history in Great spotted woodpecker extends well beyond the initial developmental stages, with several key milestones occurring several months to years after hatching. The attainment of sexual maturity, or the time since birth at puberty, occurs at 63 days since birth [tp = 63 days since birth] for individuals developing under an ambient thermal regime of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This relatively early onset of gonadal maturation is notable among woodpeckers and may be linked to the species' opportunistic breeding strategy in response to local food abundance. However, first successful reproduction is typically deferred well beyond the point of physiological maturity. The time since birth at first brood, marking the age at which a female produces her first clutch, is 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], meaning that most individuals do not breed until their second calendar year at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This delay, observed under typical field conditions, allows juveniles to acquire a high-quality territory and to develop the necessary foraging skills for provisioning young. The maximum recorded longevity for the species reaches approximately 4635 days [am = approximately 4635 days], a lifespan that places Dendrocopos major among the longer-lived picids relative to its body size, likely due to its protected cavity-nesting habit and relatively low adult mortality from predation at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C].
